You're post is a little misleading regarding the discussion of "single payer" health care systems.

In a broader context, Medicare is an example of one variety of single payer system. Anyone who currently qualifies for (and is covered by) a Medicare plan benefits from a single health insurance system that is defined as to the cost of health care services. In other words, the Medicare system determines what the maximum charge for any covered medical service will be. (I have had a number of health issues over the last four years and can speak at length on this). Payment on behalf of enrollees, can be made by the federal government or by private insurers.

While no country has a "perfect" health care system (i.e. one that no one would be unhappy with), an overlooked benefit of single payer systems is the one realized by health care service providers. To explain, prior to the ACA (and for non Medicare covered individuals), insurance providers were free to cherry pick the benefits that any given plan would provide services under (simplest example is the "prior condition" clause that prevented some people from being able to obtain any health insurance). Think about a child born with a genetic medical condition, these individuals were routinely denied coverage prior to the ACA. With the ACA. this type of discrimination is not allowed.

Additionally, under the "market defined" system (non Medicare covered individuals), health care providers had to employ larger numbers of accounting personnel in order to decipher the differences between the multitude of market plans (this is also a weakness in the current ACA system) - stated simpler, the profitable health care provider would have dedicated individuals determining the optimum manner in which to "code" a rendered service to receive the highest benefit. (Conversely, Medicare supplies a single definition for all charges covered by the Medicare system.) Think of buying a car, you've decided the make, the model, the additional packages but you still must negotiate with individual dealerships in order to find the cheapest price for the exact same vehicle.

Anyone that has talked to physicians will tell you that non Medicare health insurance (even after the ACA) suffers from this impediment to quality health care. The market based solution (from health care providers) has been the rise in "specialists" that only perform a single type of procedure. An example are orthopedic surgeons that specialize in doing vertebrae fusing operations for back pain sufferers. For a number of reasons, Florida is filled with these specialists (alright, it's because of all the old people like me that live here) that will only perform this procedure below the neck.

I could go on at length as to how the insurance industry defines health care in this country to the detriment of both providers and consumers of health care services....

Regarding payment for these systems, the first question to answer is whether or not the country is better off if all citizens have access to health care. The ACA has already shown a reduction in current and projected health care costs - is this something that the country is better off for.
